verified_symbols.name: ResolutionPlan
verified_symbols.doc: Everything that determines what a resolution round produced.

verified_symbols.name: write_plan
verified_symbols.doc:
Write the plan node (create-only, so idempotent) and return its node id.

Properties are create-only on the Tiled store, which is correct here: a
content-addressed plan never changes, and a second call with the same plan
writes the same node.

verified_symbols.name: write_activity
verified_symbols.doc:
Write one round's `stage_execution` node and its `prov:hadPlan` edge.

Call it once, when the round has finished: the timing, cost and counts are
properties of the node, and properties are create-only on the Tiled store.
The plan node must already exist (`write_plan`).

Returns:
    The activity's node id (`activity_node_id(round_key)`), which is what a
    `Decision.activity_id` carries.

Raises:
    RuntimeError: the store has no `upsert_edge`. Checked BEFORE the node is
        written, so nothing is left half-recorded.
verified_symbols.signature: store: KGStore, *, round_key: str, plan: ResolutionPlan, started: float, finished: float, counts: dict[str, int], cost_usd: float, input_tokens: int, output_tokens: int

verified_symbols.name: link_resolved_terms
verified_symbols.doc:
One `forge:resolvedTerm` edge from the activity to each term it moved edges onto.

Args:
    store: The store.
    activity_id: `write_activity`'s return value.
    targets: Canonical target node id -> number of edges moved onto it.

Returns:
    How many edges are in the store afterwards (a target the store refuses
    -- unknown node -- is logged and not counted).
verified_symbols.signature: store: KGStore, activity_id: str, targets: dict[str, int]

verified_symbols.name: git_sha
verified_symbols.doc: The code version: this checkout's HEAD sha, or "" when git cannot say.

verified_symbols.name: Unit
verified_symbols.doc: One classification unit: the thing a verdict is actually about.

verified_symbols.name: verdict_classes
verified_symbols.doc:
Every class a verdict asserts: the primary, plus any `also`.

ONE READER FOR A TWO-PART FIELD. A human may record that one image holds a
TEM micrograph AND a 1-D curve AND a simulation -- `class` carries the
primary and `also` the rest. A consumer that reads only `class` silently
sees a third of such a verdict, and the ones that matter here are
allowlists: `dual_fit_trigger` would refuse to pair a figure as a
micrograph because its PRIMARY class happened to be the 1-D curve.

Empty `also` is the overwhelmingly common case (every model verdict), so
this costs a set construction and changes nothing for them.

verified_symbols.name: panel_parents
verified_symbols.doc:
``{panel id: parent figure id}`` for every ``forge:hasPanel`` edge.

Paged to exhaustion rather than through `find_links`, which takes one
subject at a time: there are 7,310 of these edges over 1,968 figures, and
a per-figure loop would be 1,968 round trips.

verified_symbols.name: resolve_units
verified_symbols.doc:
Reduce a subject->verdict map to the units a consumer should act on.

A figure whose panels carry verdicts is SUPERSEDED: its own verdict
describes the collage, and the panels describe what is in it. Without this
the same content appears twice -- once as the composite and once per panel
-- and a reviewer cannot tell which row is which, because both arrive under
the same key.

Args:
    verdicts: ``{subject id: verdict properties}``, newest-wins, as
        `_newest_verdicts` returns. Holds figures AND panels together;
        they are indistinguishable here, which is the problem this solves.
    parents: ``{panel id: figure id}`` from :func:`panel_parents`.
    include_superseded: Keep the composite's own verdict alongside its
        panels. For a caller that wants to COMPARE the two readings rather
        than choose between them.
    panel_order: ``{panel id: index}`` from :func:`panel_order_map`, so one
        figure's panels sort the way a reader sees them. WITHOUT IT the
        order within a figure is by subject UUID, which is stable but
        arbitrary -- the index is not on the verdict (`record_classification`
        writes an allowlist and does not carry it), so it has to be read
        from the panel entities or not at all.

Returns:
    One `Unit` per acted-on subject, in a stable order (figure, then panel
    order, then subject id) so two runs agree.
verified_symbols.signature: verdicts: dict[str, dict[str, Any]], parents: dict[str, str], *, include_superseded: bool=False, panel_order: dict[str, int] | None=None

verified_symbols.name: panel_order_map
verified_symbols.doc:
``{panel id: index}``, so one figure's panels sort as a reader sees them.

READ FROM THE PANEL ENTITY, not from the verdict. The first version of this
took `verdict["panel_index"]` -- a key `record_classification` never writes,
because its properties dict is an allowlist. It would have returned 0 for
every panel while the docstring claimed the panels were ordered, which is
the "a guard no test can fail" shape this repo keeps re-learning.

Args:
    panels: Rows from `page_all_panels`; read from the graph when omitted.

verified_symbols.name: record_classification
verified_symbols.doc:
Write one classification edge from a figure to its class anchor.

Args:
    figure_entity_id: The ``paper_figure`` entity's id, as ``query_nodes``
        returns it. NOT an als node id -- those do not resolve here.
    verdict: The mapping from ``classify_figure_image``.
    anchors: Label to anchor id, from :func:`ensure_class_anchors`.
    classified_at: ISO timestamp; defaults to now, UTC.

Returns:
    True when the edge was written.
verified_symbols.signature: figure_entity_id: str, verdict: dict[str, Any], anchors: dict[str, str], *, classified_at: str | None=None

verified_symbols.name: caption_clauses
verified_symbols.doc:
A caption split into the clauses its `(a)`, `(b)` markers introduce.

WHY A COMPOSITE CAPTION IS NOT EVIDENCE ABOUT A FIGURE. Half the captioned
figures in this corpus (1,465 of 2,932) enumerate two or more panels, so a
caption naming SEM says nothing about the figure -- it says something about
one panel of it. That is what killed the deterministic tier in the figure
review queue: of 36 caption-vs-verdict disagreements that survived every
other filter, 27 were multi-panel figures whose caption named a technique
for a panel the verdict was not about.

Split, each clause belongs to exactly one panel, and the panel label
recovered from the image is the key. Measured: 1,431 of the 2,113 labelled
panels (68%) match a clause, median 67 characters.

Returns:
    Lower-cased letter -> the caption text following it, up to the next
    marker. Empty when the caption enumerates nothing.

verified_symbols.name: panel_context
verified_symbols.doc:
What to tell the classifier about one panel.

THREE CASES, AND THE MIDDLE ONE IS THE TRAP. A labelled panel gets its OWN
clause. An unlabelled one gets the figure's caption -- but LABELLED AS the
whole figure's, because handing a panel a caption that describes five
panels, without saying so, invites the model to classify the figure it came
from rather than the image in front of it. 5,197 of 7,310 panels have no
letter, so this is the common path, not the edge case.

A label with no matching clause falls back to the figure caption for the
same reason: a letter the caption never enumerates tells us nothing.
verified_symbols.signature: label: str, figure_caption: str, *, limit: int=300

verified_symbols.name: PaperContexts
verified_symbols.doc:
The paper behind each figure, read once and rendered per figure.

The rendering is PER FIGURE and the ingredients are PER PUBLICATION, which
is why this is an object rather than a mapping: the citing sentence depends
on the figure's own number, and a paper with 86 figures would otherwise hold
86 copies of its sections.

Empty is a legitimate state and means every figure is classified from its
image and caption, exactly as every sweep before this one did.

verified_symbols.name: build_paper_contexts
verified_symbols.doc:
Read the paper behind every figure, in three paged passes.

Args:
    store: The graph store. Defaults to the configured one.

Returns:
    A :class:`PaperContexts`, empty when the join found nothing.

THREE PAGED READS FOR THE WHOLE CORPUS, not three lookups per figure. The
`schema:image` edges, the publications and the sections are each one pass.
`store.get_node` costs 13.9 s against this graph because it has no
server-side id filter, so per-figure resolution is fifteen hours for 4,038
figures before a single image is read. That clamp family is recorded six
times in this repo; this is the seventh place it would have bitten.

IT DEGRADES TO EMPTY RATHER THAN RAISING. A sweep of 226,000 images must not
die because an enrichment could not be read. The cost of failing here is a
worse description, and `with_context` in the sweep counts is what says it
happened -- 0 against a graph full of `schema:image` edges means the join
failed, which is otherwise invisible because every verdict still lands.

verified_symbols.name: classify_unclassified_figures
verified_symbols.doc:
Classify every figure that has no current verdict, and report honestly.

Args:
    limit: A RUNAWAY GUARD, not a page size. The default is effectively
        "all", matching `classify_unclassified_panels` beside it -- and
        matching it is the whole point.

        IT WAS 200, AND THAT COST A SWEEP. Measured 2026-09-17: a v7 run of
        the full corpus reported `considered: 200, classified: 192` against
        4,663 figures and exited reporting success, while the panel stage of
        the SAME run did all 7,310 because its default is 100,000. Two
        sweeps in one module disagreeing about their default by a factor of
        500, and the caller passed neither.

        The graph said so and it was not heard: `iter_entities` logged
        "returned exactly 200 entities, which is its limit" at the start of
        the run. A wrong DEFAULT is invisible to every test that passes the
        argument, which is why `TestTheDefaultIsNotAUISizedClamp` asserts the
        signature rather than the behaviour.
    model: Vision model id; defaults to the configured one.
    reclassify: Re-run figures that already carry a verdict from the CURRENT
        prompt version. Off by default so a re-run is cheap and idempotent.
    concurrency: Vision calls in flight. Defaults to
        ``DEFAULT_SWEEP_CONCURRENCY``. 1 restores the old serial loop
        exactly, which is what the equivalence test compares against.

Returns:
    Counts plus a per-figure list. ``skipped_missing_image`` is reported
    SEPARATELY from ``failed`` because they call for different actions: a
    missing file needs the paper re-ingested, a failure needs the model
    looked at. Collapsing them into one number is how "the vision service is
    down" gets mistaken for "these papers are old".
verified_symbols.signature: *, limit: int=100000, model: str | None=None, reclassify: bool=False, concurrency: int | None=None

verified_symbols.name: classify_unclassified_panels
verified_symbols.doc:
Classify figure PANELS, the unit a caption clause actually describes.

WHY PANELS AND NOT FIGURES. Half this corpus's captioned figures enumerate
two or more panels, so "what is this figure" has no single answer for them
and the caption cannot settle a disagreement -- which is what left the
775-figure review queue with no deterministic tier. A panel has one answer.
Measured on a 12-panel sample: 4.4 s each against 7.4 s for a figure,
because a panel image is ~13 kB where a figure is ~190 kB.

ADDITIVE, DELIBERATELY. This writes `classifiedAs` edges FROM THE PANEL and
does not touch figure verdicts. `figure_orientation._USABLE_CLASSES`,
`dual_fit_trigger`, the review queue and the fine-tune dataset all read the
figure's class; changing which entity carries it is a design decision, and
this is not the commit that makes it.

Returns:
    Counts plus a per-panel list, in `classify_unclassified_figures`'
    shape -- `skipped_missing_image` separate from `failed`, because a
    missing file needs the paper re-ingested and a failure needs the model
    looked at.
verified_symbols.signature: *, limit: int=100000, model: str | None=None, reclassify: bool=False, concurrency: int | None=None

verified_symbols.name: panel_path
verified_symbols.doc:
The catalog path of one panel. DETERMINISTIC, so a re-run is idempotent.

The version is in the path because entity properties are create-only: a
corrected extraction cannot edit last version's panel, so it mints a new
one and the old is swept.
verified_symbols.signature: figure_entity_id: str, index: int, version: str=EXTRACTION_VERSION

verified_symbols.name: extract_figure
verified_symbols.doc:
Read one figure: its panels, their scales, their q ranges.

Args:
    figure: A `paper_figure` row from :func:`page_all_figures`.
    dry_run: Compute and report without writing anything.
    use_ocr: Read the pixels for panel letters and tick values. ON by
        default because a legacy figure has NO in-figure text without it --
        measured, 34 of the reference plate's 35 runs appear nowhere in the
        PDF's own text layer. The unit is never taken from OCR; that is
        enforced in `figure_ocr` and again in `record_figure_qrange`.

Returns:
    A per-figure report. ``status`` is ``"extracted"`` whenever the pass
    ran, INCLUDING when it found nothing -- that is a result, and the
    `hasExtraction` edge records it so a re-run can skip it.
verified_symbols.signature: figure: dict[str, Any], *, dry_run: bool=True, use_ocr: bool=True

verified_symbols.name: extract_unextracted_figures
verified_symbols.doc:
Read every figure this version has not read yet, and report honestly.

Args:
    limit: Most figures to consider in one pass.
    reextract: Re-read figures already carrying a current-version
        extraction. Off by default so a re-run is cheap and idempotent.
    dry_run: Compute and report without writing. ON by default.
    use_ocr: See :func:`extract_figure`.

Returns:
    Counts plus a per-figure list. ``skipped_missing_image`` is reported
    SEPARATELY from ``failed`` because they call for different actions: a
    missing file needs the paper re-ingested, a failure needs the code
    looked at. Collapsing them is how "the cache was moved" gets mistaken
    for "these figures are unreadable".
verified_symbols.signature: *, limit: int=200, reextract: bool=False, dry_run: bool=True, use_ocr: bool=True

verified_symbols.name: sweep_panels_of
verified_symbols.doc:
Every panel hanging off a figure, deleted before the figure itself.

THE GRANDCHILD HOLE. `corpus_refresh` walks child predicates exactly ONE
level down from the publication, so deleting a figure never sees its
panels. `deleteEntity` cascades to LINKS, not across them, so the panels
survive with their scale and q-range edges intact and nothing pointing at
them -- and they still answer a `newest_qranges` query, about a region of
an image nobody can find.

Args:
    figure_id: The `paper_figure` about to be deleted.
    apply: Delete. Off by default, like every other repair here.

Returns:
    The panel ids found, whether or not they were deleted.

verified_symbols.name: FigureTextLayer
verified_symbols.doc:
A figure's position and text, however they were obtained.

Attributes:
    frame: How page points map onto the figure PNG's pixels, or ``None``
        when the position could not be established.
    spans: The text inside the figure, in PAGE POINTS -- unclipped
        coordinates, exactly as :func:`span_to_pixels` expects.
    frame_source: ``"stored"`` (M1 stamped it at ingest), ``"template"``
        (recovered by matching the PNG onto its page) or ``""``.
    text_source: ``"sidecar"``, ``"pymupdf"`` or ``""``.
    reason: Why it is empty, when it is. Never a bare falsehood.

verified_symbols.name: figure_page
verified_symbols.doc: The 1-based page a stored figure came from, read off its filename.

verified_symbols.name: pdf_for_figure
verified_symbols.doc:
The PDF a cached figure was cut out of, or ``None``.

Figures live in ``<cache>/<stem>_images/<stem>-pNNN-MM.png`` beside
``<cache>/<stem>.pdf``. Derived rather than stored because the 4,028
existing figures record only their own path.

verified_symbols.name: locate_figure_on_page
verified_symbols.doc:
Where the stored PNG sits on its page, in PAGE POINTS, and why not.

Args:
    image_path: The cached figure PNG.
    document: An open pymupdf document.
    page_index: 0-based page index.

Returns:
    ``(bbox, reason)`` with bbox as ``(left, top, right, bottom)`` in page
    points, TOPLEFT origin -- pymupdf's own convention, and the one the
    rendered pixels are indexed in. ``(None, reason)`` when the figure
    could not be placed: ``"unreadable_image"``, ``"image_larger_than_page"``,
    ``"weak_match"`` or ``"ambiguous_match"``.
verified_symbols.signature: image_path: str | Path, document: Any, page_index: int

verified_symbols.name: text_layer_for
verified_symbols.doc:
A figure's frame and text, from the sidecar if M1 wrote one, else the PDF.

THE PDF IS OPENED EITHER WAY, even when the sidecar is present and the bbox
is stored. It is the only independent witness to which sidecar spans came
from the PDF's own text layer and which RapidOCR read off the pixels, and
that distinction decides whether a q-axis unit may be believed. Skipping
the open when the sidecar looks complete would make the fast path the
dishonest one.

Args:
    figure: A `paper_figure` entity's flattened properties -- ``path`` and,
        for post-M1 rows, ``bbox``, ``images_scale`` and ``spans_path``.
    size_px: The PNG's ``(width, height)``, when the caller has already
        loaded it. Read from the file otherwise.

Returns:
    A :class:`FigureTextLayer`. Never raises for a figure it cannot read:
    an unrecoverable figure is a recorded outcome, not an exception, or a
    batch over 4,028 rows stops at the first malformed one.
verified_symbols.signature: figure: dict[str, Any], *, size_px: tuple[int, int] | None=None

verified_symbols.name: detect
verified_symbols.doc:
Run OCR ONCE and hand back its rows as ``(text, pixel box, confidence)``.

Both readers here parse the same detections, and a figure is only worth
scanning once: at 0.31 s a figure, calling the engine twice adds twenty
minutes to a 4,028-row backfill for no new information.

Returns empty on any failure -- an unreadable figure is a recorded outcome,
not an exception that stops the pass.

verified_symbols.name: read_bar_labels
verified_symbols.doc:
The lengths printed beside scale bars, as page-point spans.

SEPARATE FROM :func:`read_figure_text`, AND DELIBERATELY SO. That function
reports only single letters and bare numbers, because a mangled unit there
becomes a wrong q range. This one must report a unit to be worth anything
at all, so it is a different function with a different, much narrower
grammar, and a caller has to ask for it by name.

MEASURED on the 30 bar-mentioning figures checked: 11 carry a label OCR
reads cleanly -- "100 nm", "1.25 um", "400nm", "50 nm" -- at 0.92 to 1.00.
The residual risk is nm read as um, a factor of a thousand, and it is
handled by PROVENANCE rather than by pretending it cannot happen:
`read_panel_scale` stamps such a reading ``length_source="ocr"``, the graph
stores `source="ocr"`, and that is the lowest rank in `SCALE_SOURCES`, below
every number a human or an author supplied.

Args:
    image: The figure as an RGB array, in its own pixels.
    frame: How those pixels map back onto page points.
    engine: Injectable for tests.

Returns:
    Spans stamped ``source="ocr"``. Feed them to `read_panel_scale` as
    `length_spans`; do NOT put them in the pool an axis fit reads, where
    the number in "500 nm" is one more tick.
verified_symbols.signature: image: Any, frame: FigureFrame, *, engine: Any=None, detections: tuple[Detection, ...] | None=None

verified_symbols.name: read_figure_text
verified_symbols.doc:
Panel letters and tick values painted into a figure, as page-point spans.

Args:
    image: The figure as an RGB array, in its own pixels.
    frame: How those pixels map back onto page points, so OCR spans and
        text-layer spans can live in one list.
    engine: Injectable for tests. The shared engine otherwise.
    detections: Rows from a :func:`detect` call the caller already made, so
        one scan can serve both readers.

Returns:
    Spans stamped ``source="ocr"``, in page points. Empty when OCR is
    unavailable or finds nothing it may report -- never an exception, so a
    batch over 4,028 figures does not stop at one unreadable image.
verified_symbols.signature: image: Any, frame: FigureFrame, *, engine: Any=None, detections: tuple[Detection, ...] | None=None

verified_symbols.name: record_figure_scale
verified_symbols.doc:
Append one scale reading for a figure.

Args:
    figure_entity_id: The `paper_figure` entity, by its graph id.
    extent_nm: The figure's field of view in nm -- what the scale bar or the
        axis range says the image spans.
    source: One of :data:`SCALE_SOURCES`.
    reviewer: Who read it. Free text; empty for a non-human source.
    note: Which bar, which axis, which caption sentence.
    needs_review: Ask for a human look. Set by the caller for its own
        reasons, and set HERE regardless when the extent falls outside
        :data:`PLAUSIBLE_EXTENT_NM` -- an impossible field of view is
        stored rather than refused, because the reading is evidence that
        something was misread and deleting it loses that.
    recorded_at: ISO timestamp; defaults to now, UTC.

Returns:
    True when the edge was written.

Raises:
    ValueError: If the extent is not a positive finite number, or the source
        is unrecognised. A non-positive extent is not a degenerate scale --
        it is no scale at all, and storing it would let a fit run in units
        that do not exist.
verified_symbols.signature: figure_entity_id: str, extent_nm: float, *, source: str='human', reviewer: str='', note: str='', needs_review: bool=False, recorded_at: str | None=None

verified_symbols.name: newest_scales
verified_symbols.doc:
Newest scale reading per figure, by `recorded_at`.

A thin call into :func:`forge.kg.views.newest_link_properties`, which is
the ONE implementation of newest-wins-by-append. This used to carry its own
copy of that paging loop; there were four such copies in the tree, and four
places for the tie-breaking, the pagination and the JSON-string handling to
drift apart from each other.

verified_symbols.name: record_figure_qrange
verified_symbols.doc:
Append one q-range reading for a figure or one of its panels.

Args:
    entity_id: A `paper_figure` OR a `figure_panel`, by its graph id. Both
        are valid subjects, and a composite figure's range belongs on the
        panel: one figure holds one range, and a plate of nine patterns at
        different sample-detector distances has nine.
    q_min_nm_inv: Low end of the band, in inverse nanometres, ALREADY
        folded. Angstrom^-1 arrives here multiplied by ten or not at all.
    q_max_nm_inv: High end, same units.
    unit_source: One of :data:`QRANGE_UNIT_SOURCES`.
    axis_kind: One of :data:`QRANGE_AXIS_KINDS`.
    n_ticks: How many ticks the fit used. A reviewer's first question.
    confidence: Fit quality, 0-1.
    note: Which axis, which panel, which caption sentence.
    extraction_version: The extractor that read it, so a re-read at a newer
        version is distinguishable from a re-read at the same one.
    needs_review: Whether a human should look, even though a value exists.
    recorded_at: ISO timestamp; defaults to now, UTC.

Returns:
    True when the edge was written.

Raises:
    ValueError: If the range is not a positive, strictly increasing, finite
        pair; if the unit source is not one this may believe -- an
        OCR-sourced unit is refused HERE rather than trusted to a caller,
        because the whole value of the reading rests on it; or if the axis
        kind is unrecognised.
verified_symbols.signature: entity_id: str, q_min_nm_inv: float, q_max_nm_inv: float, *, unit_source: str, axis_kind: str='linear', n_ticks: int=0, confidence: float=0.0, note: str='', extraction_version: str='', needs_review: bool=False, recorded_at: str | None=None

verified_symbols.name: newest_qranges
verified_symbols.doc:
Newest q-range reading per subject, by `recorded_at`.

Subjects are figures AND panels mixed, deliberately: a caller pairing
figures wants whichever of the two carries the reading, and separating them
here would make every caller re-join them.

verified_symbols.name: parse_orientation_answer
verified_symbols.doc:
Map a model reply to the extraction schema's orientation vocabulary.

Args:
    raw: The model's text.

Returns:
    ``"parallel"`` (layers flat -> out-of-plane reflection),
    ``"perpendicular"`` (layers on edge -> in-plane reflection), or ``""``
    for UNCLEAR, an empty reply, or anything unrecognised.

THE TWO VOCABULARIES ARE INVERSE-SOUNDING AND THAT IS THE HAZARD. A reading
of OUT_OF_PLANE means the layers are PARALLEL to the substrate, because what
is out-of-plane is the layer NORMAL, not the layers. Asking the model about
the reflection rather than about the layers is deliberate: the reflection is
what it can see, and the one inversion then happens here, once, in code that
a test can pin.

verified_symbols.name: candidate_subjects
verified_symbols.doc:
Images to ask, best first: scattering PANELS, then whole figures.

ASKING A COMPOSITE IS ASKING A COLLAGE. `ORIENTATION_PROMPT` shows an image
and asks where the strongest non-specular feature sits -- a question with no
answer about a grid of a chemical structure, an AFM height map and a GISAXS
pattern. 44% of this corpus's panelled figures hold panels that disagree
with each other, so for those the composite is exactly the wrong thing to
send. A panel classified `experimental_scattering` is one pattern, and the
question means what it says.

It is also a RECALL fix, because the old selector could not see a class at
all (see `_is_usable`). Measured on the live graph: caption hints alone
reach 300 figures across 204 publications; the stored verdicts reach 406
figures and 830 panels across 278, of which 115 publications were
unreachable before.

Ordering is deliberate and is the whole point: every panel comes before
every whole figure, so the first image the model sees is the most specific
one available. Caption-only figures come last -- they are a guess about
content, where a verdict is a reading of it.

Args:
    publication_id: The publication's node id, as figures record it.
    verdicts / parents / figures / panels: Injected for tests; read from the
        graph when omitted. All four together are one pass over the corpus,
        so a caller doing several papers should read once and pass them in.

Returns:
    Best-first candidates. Empty is a real answer: this paper shows no
    2-D scattering image.
verified_symbols.signature: publication_id: str, *, verdicts: dict[str, dict[str, Any]] | None=None, parents: dict[str, str] | None=None, figures: list[dict[str, Any]] | None=None, panels: list[dict[str, Any]] | None=None

verified_symbols.name: read_lamellar_orientation
verified_symbols.doc:
Ask the vision model which way a paper's lamellae lie.

Args:
    publication_id: The publication's node id, as figures record it.
    model: Vision model id; defaults to the configured one.

Returns:
    ``(orientation, detail)``. *orientation* is ``"parallel"``,
    ``"perpendicular"`` or ``""``; *detail* always says what happened, so a
    caller can log why it got nothing. NEVER RAISES.

verified_symbols.name: TextSpan
verified_symbols.doc:
One run of text inside a figure, with where it sits.

Attributes:
    text: The run, VERBATIM. Never normalised here -- the superscript in
        ``'(Å -1 )'`` is the Angstrom-versus-nanometre decider, and a
        pipeline that tidied it on the way in would destroy the one signal
        OCR cannot supply.
    bbox: ``(left, top, right, bottom)`` in the span's own coordinates.
        ``None`` when the parser gave no provenance -- the text is still
        useful (a unit, a caption fragment) with no position.
    page: Page the run sits on.
    source: ``"text_layer"`` (the PDF's own) or ``"ocr"``. LOAD-BEARING:
        a unit may only be believed from the text layer, so anything that
        reads a unit has to be able to tell them apart.

verified_symbols.name: PanelBox
verified_symbols.doc:
One panel of a figure, in the figure PNG's own pixel coordinates.

Attributes:
    left / top / right / bottom: Pixel bounds, top-left origin, as the
        image itself is indexed.
    label: The panel letter, or ``""`` when the figure marks none. An
        unlabelled panel is still a panel.
    method: How it was found -- ``"text_layer"``, ``"gutter"`` or
        ``"whole_figure"`` (a single-panel figure standing as its own).

verified_symbols.name: ScaleReading
verified_symbols.doc:
A figure or panel's scale, or the named reason it has none.

Attributes:
    nm_per_px: The answer, or ``None``.
    bar_length_px: Measured bar length.
    bar_length_nm: What the bar was said to be.
    length_source: Where the NANOMETRES came from -- ``"caption"``,
        ``"text_layer"`` or ``"ocr"``. The pixels are always measured; this
        names the half that was read, and it decides the provenance the
        graph stores.
    reason: ``""`` on success, else e.g. ``"no_bar"``,
        ``"bar_without_length"``, ``"multiple_bars_one_length"``.
    needs_review: A human should look, even if a value was produced.
    review_reasons: Why, in the classifier's vocabulary.

verified_symbols.name: QAxisReading
verified_symbols.doc:
A scattering figure's q range, in inverse nanometres, or why not.

Attributes:
    q_min_nm_inv / q_max_nm_inv: The range, or ``None``.
    unit_source: ``"text_layer"`` or ``"caption"`` ONLY. An OCR-sourced
        unit is refused upstream and never reaches here -- RapidOCR was
        measured to mangle the exponent on 100% of attempts, and getting it
        wrong is a factor of ten that lands on a plausible number.
    axis_kind: ``"linear"`` or ``"log"``.
    n_ticks: How many ticks the fit used.
    confidence: Fit quality, 0-1.
    reason / needs_review / review_reasons: As for :class:`ScaleReading`.

verified_symbols.name: FigureFrame
verified_symbols.doc:
The mapping from one figure's page-point box into its PNG pixels.

Args:
    bbox: ``(left, top, right, bottom)`` in page points, as
        ``BoundingBox.as_dict()`` records them.
    images_scale: Rendered pixels per point.
    coord_origin: ``"BOTTOMLEFT"`` (docling's PDF-native default) or
        ``"TOPLEFT"``.
    size_px: ``(width, height)`` of the saved PNG, when known. Used only to
        clip; absent means no clipping.

Raises:
    ValueError: If the scale is not positive, or the box is degenerate in
        either axis. A zero-width figure cannot map anything and would
        divide by nothing later.

verified_symbols.name: span_to_pixels
verified_symbols.doc:
A span's box in figure-PNG pixels, or ``None`` if it has no box.

Args:
    span: The text run.
    frame: The figure it sits in.

Returns:
    ``(left, top, right, bottom)`` in pixels, top-left origin and already
    ordered so ``top < bottom`` whichever way the source counted. ``None``
    when the span carries no bbox -- which is a real case, not an error:
    a run without provenance still carries usable text.

verified_symbols.name: spans_inside
verified_symbols.doc:
The spans whose CENTRE falls inside a pixel region.

Centre rather than any overlap: a scale-bar label sitting on a panel
boundary belongs to the panel it is mostly in, and an overlap rule would
hand the same label to two panels and let both claim a scale from it.

Args:
    spans: Candidate runs.
    frame: The figure they sit in.
    region: ``(left, top, right, bottom)`` in figure-PNG pixels.

Returns:
    The subset whose centre is inside. Spans with no bbox are EXCLUDED --
    the question is positional and they cannot answer it.
verified_symbols.signature: spans: list[TextSpan], frame: FigureFrame, region: tuple[float, float, float, float]

verified_symbols.name: panel_labels
verified_symbols.doc:
Every distinct panel letter *caption* marks, lowercased.

Args:
    caption: The figure's caption text.

Returns:
    The letters found, in no particular order. An empty set means the
    caption marks no panels, which is NOT the same as the figure having
    one panel -- a caption can describe a composite without lettering it,
    and this reads prose only.

verified_symbols.name: caption_names_multiple_panels
verified_symbols.doc:
Does this caption describe more than one panel?

The question a per-figure value has to answer before it may be stored.
Two or more DISTINCT letters, so a caption mentioning "(a)" repeatedly is
still one panel.

Args:
    caption: The figure's caption text.

Returns:
    True when at least two distinct panel letters appear.

verified_symbols.name: ink_mask
verified_symbols.doc:
Which pixels of a greyscale figure are content rather than page.

The background is the MEDIAN OF THE BORDER RING, not of the whole image:
a dense micrograph is mostly dark, and its median is a picture value. The
ring is the page the figure was pasted onto.

Args:
    image: Greyscale figure, 2-D, any numeric dtype.

Returns:
    A boolean array, True where the pixel is ink.

Raises:
    ValueError: If *image* is not 2-D.

verified_symbols.name: segment_panels
verified_symbols.doc:
Split a figure into panel boxes along its whitespace gutters.

Two alternating cuts, never more: the figure is divided along whichever
axis carries the widest gutter, then each band is divided along the other
-- the shape a published plate actually has. The depth is fixed rather than
configurable because MEASURED a third level only ever split a line plot
along the white gaps between its own stacked curves.

THE SECOND CUT IS CROSS-CHECKED against the sibling bands
(:data:`MIN_SIBLING_AGREEMENT`). A gutter that separates panels is empty
right across the figure; a gap between two stacked curves inside one plot
is empty only there. Without the check the reference plate's line plot
shreds into four strips, each of which would then be crop, classified and
scaled as though it were a panel.

Args:
    image: Greyscale figure in the PNG's own pixel coordinates.

Returns:
    At least one box, in reading order. A figure with no gutters -- a lone
    micrograph -- comes back as ONE box with ``method="whole_figure"``,
    which is the truthful answer and the one every consumer already
    handles. Labels are NOT set here; geometry says where, never which.

verified_symbols.name: consecutive_from_a
verified_symbols.doc:
The unbroken run of panel letters starting at ``a``.

Figures letter their panels consecutively. That is a real, checkable
property of published work, and it is the only cheap way to tell a real
marker from a misread one when both are single letters sitting inside a
panel.

MEASURED on the reference plate: OCR reads its panels as
``{a, b, c, d, e, f, g, h, j}`` -- the ``j`` being a misread of a glyph the
page prints as ``i``. Nothing about the ``j`` looks wrong on its own: it is
a single letter, confidently read, inside exactly one box. What gives it
away is the GAP. There is no ``i``, so ``j`` cannot be the tenth panel of
a figure whose ninth is missing.

Args:
    labels: Candidate letters, in any order and any case.

Returns:
    The letters from ``a`` up to the first gap. Empty when there is no
    ``a`` -- a figure whose lettering does not start at the beginning is
    not one this can reason about, and guessing where it starts would admit
    every misread letter on the page.

verified_symbols.name: reconcile_panels
verified_symbols.doc:
Settle the caption's panel letters against the geometry's panel boxes.

The two sources answer different questions and neither answers both. The
caption says HOW MANY panels there are and what they are called; it never
says where. The gutters say where; they cannot tell a panel from a plot
that happens to have a white band across it.

WHEN THEY DISAGREE, THE FIGURE STANDS WHOLE. A caption naming four panels
against three boxes means one boundary is wrong, and there is no way to
know which -- pairing them anyway would hand some panel its neighbour's
scale bar, a wrong number with a real provenance chain behind it. One
unsplit figure is recoverable; a mislabelled crop is a fabrication.

Args:
    boxes: Geometry's answer, from :func:`segment_panels`.
    labels: Panel letters from the caption, e.g. :func:`panel_labels`.
    shape: The figure's ``(height, width)`` in pixels.

Returns:
    Labelled boxes when the counts agree; the geometry unlabelled when the
    caption names fewer than two panels and so challenges nothing; a single
    ``method="whole_figure"`` box when they disagree.
verified_symbols.signature: boxes: list[PanelBox], labels: Iterable[str], shape: tuple[int, int]

verified_symbols.name: label_panels_from_spans
verified_symbols.doc:
Letter the panels from the figure's OWN text layer, by position.

Better than the caption in every way that matters, when it is there: the
letters come with coordinates, so a panel gets the letter printed INSIDE
it rather than the one that happens to fall at its place in reading order.
MEASURED on the reference plate, whose caption letters its panels as
``"a: phi = 1.0; b: phi = 0.750"`` -- a style no caption matcher here reads
-- while the text layer puts a bare ``'a'`` at the top-right of the first
grid cell.

A BOX HOLDING SEVERAL MARKERS IS NOT LABELLED, and that rule is why this is
safe. On the same plate the tall line plot is a stack of nine curves, each
annotated with the letter of the grid panel it corresponds to: eight
single-letter spans inside one box. Taking the first, or the topmost, would
name that panel after a curve drawn inside it. Ambiguity here is real
information -- it says this box is not a lettered panel -- and it is kept.

THE SPANS CAN LIE, and *allowed* is the cheap defence. MEASURED on the
reference plate: its third grid column reads as ``'J'`` where the page
prints ``c``, ``f`` and ``i``. That was first written up here as a
font-encoding fault in the PDF; it is not. Docling runs OCR by default
(`PdfPipelineOptions.do_ocr` is True), in-figure lettering in published
papers is usually rasterised into the image, and 34 of that figure's 35
spans have no counterpart anywhere in the PDF's own text layer. The bad
letters are OCR misreads. Nothing in the geometry can tell one from a real
letter, so a caller holding an independent alphabet passes it and a marker
outside it is ignored.

Args:
    boxes: Panels from :func:`segment_panels`.
    spans: The figure's text layer, in page points.
    frame: How those points map onto the figure's pixels.
    allowed: The only letters that may be believed. Empty means believe
        any single letter, which is right when there is nothing to check
        against and wrong the moment there is.

Returns:
    The boxes, in the order given, each labelled where exactly one marker
    sits inside it and no other box claims the same letter.
verified_symbols.signature: boxes: list[PanelBox], spans: list[TextSpan], frame: FigureFrame, allowed: Iterable[str]=()

verified_symbols.name: AxisCandidate
verified_symbols.doc:
A run of numeric ticks sharing one coordinate.

Attributes:
    orientation: ``"x"`` (a row of ticks, value varying with pixel x) or
        ``"y"`` (a column).
    ticks: ``(value, position_px)`` pairs, position along the varying axis.

verified_symbols.name: find_axis_candidates
verified_symbols.doc:
Group a panel's numeric spans into rows and columns.

Args:
    spans: Runs from ONE panel. Passing a whole figure's spans merges the
        axes of side-by-side panels -- measured, and it produces a slope
        through two unrelated ranges.
    tolerance_px: How far apart two ticks' shared coordinate may be and
        still count as one axis.

Returns:
    Every candidate with at least :data:`MIN_AXIS_TICKS` ticks, largest
    first. Spans with no bbox are skipped: an axis is a geometric claim.

verified_symbols.name: read_q_axis
verified_symbols.doc:
The q range this panel's axis states, in inverse nanometres.

THE UNIT IS THE BOTTLENECK, MEASURED. Over 60 sampled scattering figures
(236 panels): `no_unit` 221, `no_axis` 12, `no_positive_ticks` 2, determined
1. The ticks read fine; what is missing is what they MEAN. Only 2 of those
60 captions stated a unit.

So three sources are tried, MOST SPECIFIC FIRST -- this panel's own axis
text, then this figure's caption, then the paper's prose. Each is recorded
in `unit_source`, because they are not equally strong evidence and a
reviewer ranking two readings needs to know which was used.

Args:
    spans: Runs from ONE panel (see :func:`find_axis_candidates`).
    caption_unit: A unit taken from the caption, used only when the text
        layer states none. Both are acceptable provenance; OCR is not.
    document_unit: A unit taken from the PAPER's section text. **NOT USED
        BY THE EXTRACTION PIPELINE, and a reading that rests on it CANNOT
        BE STORED** -- `record_figure_qrange` refuses `unit_source
        ="sections"`, which is not in `QRANGE_UNIT_SOURCES`.

        It exists because the coverage is real (4% of scattering figures
        get a unit from a caption; 44% would get one from their paper) and
        because enabling it revealed the actual blocker: nothing here checks
        that the axis `find_axis_candidates` found IS the q axis. It groups
        numeric spans geometrically. With a unit available 11x more often,
        one 60-figure sample produced a Solar Physics figure at "50-80
        nm^-1", panels at "100-105" and "100-500", and a log axis at
        "0.1-1000" -- intensity and temperature axes fitted and labelled q,
        every one at r^2 > 0.9999 with full provenance.

        Q-AXIS IDENTIFICATION IS THE MISSING PIECE, not the unit. Wire this
        up once an axis can be shown to be q -- by its title, by a physical
        bound, or both -- and admit "sections" at the storage boundary then.

Returns:
    A :class:`QAxisReading`. ``q_min``/``q_max`` are the SMALLEST and
    LARGEST LABELLED TICK, not an extrapolation to the panel edge -- the
    axis may run past its last tick, and inventing that margin would report
    a range the figure never claims. The result is therefore a
    conservative inner bound, which is the safe direction for an overlap
    test.

    Every refusal is named: ``"no_axis"``, ``"poor_fit"``, ``"no_unit"``.
verified_symbols.signature: spans: list[TextSpan], *, caption_unit: str='', document_unit: str=''

verified_symbols.name: caption_bar_lengths
verified_symbols.doc:
Every length the caption states AS A SCALE BAR, with where it was said.

Args:
    caption: The figure's caption.
    window: Maximum character gap between the phrase "scale bar" and the
        length, in either direction.

Returns:
    ``(nanometres, character_offset)`` pairs in the order written. The
    offset is kept because pairing a length to a panel depends on their
    relative POSITIONS in the prose, and sorting would destroy the only
    signal the caption gives.

    An empty list means the caption states no bar length -- which is a real
    and common case (28 of 108 bar-mentioning captions name no number at
    all) and NOT a failure.

verified_symbols.name: pair_lengths_to_panels
verified_symbols.doc:
Which panel each stated bar length belongs to, where that is decidable.

THE 42 CAPTIONS A PER-FIGURE SCALE CANNOT HOLD. "Scale bars are 2 um and
0.2 um in (a) and (b), respectively" states two scales; a figure node holds
one, so storing either asserts a falsehood about the other panel.

The rule is deliberately narrow: pair only when the number of stated bar
lengths equals the number of distinct panel letters, and pair them IN
ORDER. That covers "respectively" and the per-panel inline form
("(A) ... Scale bar, 100 nm. (B) ... Scale bar, 5 nm") and refuses
everything else.

Args:
    caption: The figure's caption.

Returns:
    ``{panel_letter: nanometres}``, or an EMPTY DICT when the pairing is
    not decidable. Empty means "this caption does not say", never "these
    panels have no scale" -- a caller must not read one as the other.

verified_symbols.name: read_panel_scale
verified_symbols.doc:
Measure one panel's bar and pair it with a length.

Args:
    image: The FIGURE as a 2-D greyscale array. The panel is cropped from
        it here rather than by the caller, so the crop and the panel box
        cannot disagree.
    panel: Where the panel sits, in figure-PNG pixels.
    caption_length_nm: The length the caption assigns to THIS panel, if the
        caller resolved one (see :func:`pair_lengths_to_panels`).
    length_spans: Text runs already known to sit inside this panel. The
        first that parses to a length is used, and it OUTRANKS the caption:
        a number printed beside the bar describes that bar, where a caption
        describes a figure and had to be apportioned.
    saturation: Grey level counted as bar.

Returns:
    A :class:`ScaleReading`. Every refusal is NAMED -- ``"no_bar"``,
    ``"multiple_bars"``, ``"bar_without_length"``, ``"panel_too_small"`` --
    because a silent skip and a considered refusal look identical in a
    report and only one of them can be trusted.
verified_symbols.signature: image: object, panel: PanelBox, *, caption_length_nm: float | None=None, length_spans: list[TextSpan] | None=None, saturation: int=250

verified_symbols.name: normalise_unit
verified_symbols.doc:
Fold one written unit onto a table key.

Args:
    text: The unit as it appeared, e.g. ``"Å -1"``, ``"µm"``, ``"m m"``.

Returns:
    A lowercase key: the micro signs become ``u``, the angstrom signs
    become ``a``, superscript minus/one become ASCII, ``^`` and stray
    spaces around an exponent are dropped, and a trailing plural ``s`` is
    removed. ``"m m"`` is preserved as itself, since it is a real spelling
    rather than a spacing artefact this can safely collapse.

verified_symbols.name: fold_length
verified_symbols.doc:
A length and its written unit, in nanometres.

Args:
    value: The magnitude, already parsed.
    unit: The unit as written, in any spelling.

Returns:
    Nanometres, or ``None`` when the unit is not one this understands or
    the value is not positive. ``None`` is a REFUSAL and never a default: a
    caption whose unit cannot be read has no length this may report, and
    guessing nanometres would be wrong by a factor of 1,000 for a
    micrometre bar.

verified_symbols.name: fold_inverse_length
verified_symbols.doc:
An inverse length and its written unit, in inverse nanometres.

Args:
    value: The magnitude.
    unit: The unit as written, e.g. ``"Å^-1"``, ``"nm⁻¹"``.

Returns:
    Inverse nanometres, or ``None``. An angstrom-inverse read as a
    nanometre-inverse is a structure ten times too large, landing on a
    plausible number, which is why an unrecognised unit refuses rather than
    assuming the commoner one.

verified_symbols.name: caption_inverse_unit
verified_symbols.doc:
The inverse-length unit a caption states, folded, or ``""``.

THE SECOND ACCEPTABLE PROVENANCE FOR A UNIT, and for most of this corpus
the only one. In-figure axis titles are usually rasterised into the image,
so pymupdf finds no unit inside the figure and OCR mangles the exponent
every time -- measured, RapidOCR renders one plate's q axis as
``'q2 [A{]}'``. The caption is prose in the PDF's own text layer, which
means it is readable and it is not a transcription.

Args:
    caption: The figure's caption.

Returns:
    A key :func:`fold_inverse_length` accepts, e.g. ``"nm-1"`` or
    ``"a-1"``. Empty when the caption states no inverse-length unit, or
    states something that only looks like one -- a caption naming BOTH
    gives nothing, because a figure whose caption says angstrom in one
    sentence and nanometre in another does not tell you which axis is
    which, and picking the first is a coin flip on a factor of ten.

verified_symbols.name: document_inverse_unit
verified_symbols.doc:
The inverse-length unit a PAPER states, folded, or ``""``.

THE THIRD ACCEPTABLE PROVENANCE, and the one that makes this readable at
all. Measured on the 998 figures holding scattering content: a caption
yields a unit for **40 of them (4.0%)**, and the panels underneath refuse
with ``no_unit`` 94% of the time -- the ticks read fine, the unit is what is
missing. The same regex over the PAPER's own section text yields exactly one
unit for 175 of 412 publications, covering **435 figures (43.6%)**.

IT IS THE SAME KIND OF EVIDENCE AS A CAPTION, which is why it is allowed:
docling section text is prose out of the PDF's own text layer. It is not a
transcription, so it does not carry the failure that bars OCR here -- a
mangled exponent turning angstrom into nanometre, a factor of ten that lands
on a plausible number.

IT IS WEAKER THAN A CAPTION, which is why it is a SEPARATE source rather
than folded in. A caption describes one figure; a paper's prose describes a
paper, and a paper may plot two things on two axes. That risk is handled the
only honest way available: **exactly one unit, or nothing.** A document
naming both angstrom and nanometre gives ``""`` -- the same coin-flip
refusal `caption_inverse_unit` already makes, for the same reason. 16 of
412 publications land there.

Args:
    texts: The paper's section texts, in any order.

Returns:
    A key :func:`fold_inverse_length` accepts, or ``""``.

verified_symbols.name: iter_lengths
verified_symbols.doc:
Every length in *text*, in nanometres, in the order written.

Args:
    text: Caption prose, or a text-layer run.

Returns:
    The lengths this could read. Unreadable units are SKIPPED rather than
    raising -- a caption naming one bar and one unrelated wavelength should
    yield the bar, not an error -- so a caller that needs to know the
    caption was fully understood must compare against its own expectation.

verified_symbols.doc:
Upsert an experimental technique node.

The node id is ``technique:<slug>``.

Upsert an analysis method node.

The node id is ``analysis:<slug>``.

    method: Human-readable method name (stored as node name).
    software: Optional software tool used for this analysis.
    source_pub_id: Optional publication node id that is the evidence source.
    confidence: Confidence score stored in node properties.

Returns:
    The node id string ``f"analysis:{slug}"``.
verified_symbols.signature: store: KGStore, slug: str, method: str, *, software: str | None=None, source_pub_id: str | None=None, confidence: float=0.9

verified_symbols.name: upsert_instrument
verified_symbols.doc:
Upsert an instrument node.

The node id is ``instrument:<slug>``.

Args:
    store: Open :class:`KGStore` instance.
    slug: Normalized instrument slug, e.g. ``"pilatus"``.
    name: Canonical display name.
    source_pub_id: Optional publication node id that is the evidence source.

Returns:

verified_symbols.signature: store: KGStore, slug: str, name: str, *, source_pub_id: str | None=None

verified_symbols.name: upsert_publication_full
verified_symbols.doc:
Upsert a publication node from an OpenAlex ``works`` record.

Mirrors the publication + author upsert logic used in the
``publication_linker`` stage of
:func:`~als_knowledge_agent.graph.enrichment_agent.run_enrichment`
(lines ~685–747).  Also upserts author nodes and ``authored_by`` edges.

Args:
    store: Open :class:`KGStore` instance.
    work: Dict representation of an OpenAlex ``works`` API response item,
        or any dict with compatible keys (``doi``, ``openalex_id``,
        ``title``, ``year``, ``citations``, ``abstract``,
        ``abstract_snippet``, ``authors``, ``journal``, ``concepts``,
        ``referenced_works``, ``referenced_works_count``).

Returns:
    The publication node id, e.g. ``"publication:W1234567890"``.

verified_symbols.name: upsert_authors
verified_symbols.doc:
Mint ``author`` nodes and ``authored_by`` edges for one publication.

EXTRACTED SO A BACKFILL CAN REACH IT. ``upsert_publication_full`` returns
EARLY when the paper already exists -- correctly, since properties are
create-only and re-minting would duplicate the paper -- and that early
return sits ABOVE this loop. So no amount of re-ingesting adds authors to a
paper already in the graph: the call returns a valid publication id and
writes nothing, which reads as success.

That matters because ``paper_resolver`` never mapped the OpenAlex
``authorships`` field onto the ``authors`` key this reads, so all 494
publications in the graph were written with an empty list. Fixing the
mapping corrects future ingests; only a backfill through this function can
reach the papers already written.

Args:
    known: Author node id -> current ``paper_count``, supplied by a caller
        that has already read them in bulk. **This is the difference
        between minutes and half a day.** ``store.get_node`` has no id
        filter on the server, so a single lookup PAGES THE WHOLE ENTITY
        TABLE: measured at 13.9 s against 35,850 entities, hit or miss,
        while ``upsert_node`` costs 0.04 s and ``upsert_edge`` 0.07 s. One
        lookup per author put a 494-paper backfill on an eleven-hour
        trajectory -- the same shape as the panel mint that
        ``upsert_entity_id`` was added to fix. One bulk
        ``query_nodes(entity_type="author")`` costs 0.03 s and answers
        every lookup. The map is UPDATED in place, so counts stay right
        across a run. Omit it and the slow path is used, which is correct
        for a one-paper ingest.

Returns:
    The number of ``authored_by`` edges written.
verified_symbols.signature: store: KGStore, pub_id: str, authors_list: list[dict[str, Any]], *, cited_as: str='', known: dict[str, int] | None=None

verified_symbols.name: upsert_material
verified_symbols.doc:
Upsert a material node. The node id is ``material:<slug>``.

THIS DID NOT EXIST, and its absence is why the live graph holds 13 material
nodes against 5,813 technique edges. Extraction has always returned materials
-- `PM6`, `BTP-eC9`, `1,3,5-trichlorobenzene` were observed coming back from
the model -- and nothing wrote them: `link_paper_to_extractions` has three
loops (techniques, analyses, instruments) and a `counts["materials"]` that is
initialised to 0 and never incremented. The 13 that exist were written by
`paper_simulation`, not by extraction.

`name` is passed through because `node_id_to_path` keys materials at
``materials/<slug(name)>`` -- so a material extraction finds converges with
the paper_simulation nodes when the names agree, rather than shadowing them.

Args:
    store: Open :class:`KGStore` instance.
    slug: Canonical vocabulary slug, e.g. ``"silica"``.
    name: Display name, e.g. ``"Silica"``.
    source_pub_id: Optional publication node id that is the evidence source.
    confidence: Confidence score stored in node properties.

Returns:
    The node id string ``f"material:{slug}"``.
verified_symbols.signature: store: KGStore, slug: str, name: str, *, source_pub_id: str | None=None, confidence: float=0.9

verified_symbols.name: upsert_candidate_term
verified_symbols.doc:
Upsert a `candidate_term` node for a term the vocabulary does not know.

The node id is ``candidate_term:<slug>``, which makes its derived path
``candidate_term/<slug>`` -- MATCHING its entity type. That is deliberate:
`technique:<slug>` derives ``technique/<slug>`` while its type is
``experimental_technique``, and that mismatch is precisely what blinds
`forge.kg.repair.find_shadow_duplicates` to the 285 duplicate technique
nodes. A new type should not inherit that.

Properties are create-only on this store, which is fine here: everything
recorded is an immutable observation of the first sighting. The adjudication
lives in the reviewed cleanup file, not on the node.
verified_symbols.signature: store: KGStore, term: ResolvedTerm, *, source_pub_id: str | None=None, model_used: str | None=None

verified_symbols.name: current_vocabulary_version
verified_symbols.doc:
The vocabulary these edges were resolved against.

STAMPED ALONGSIDE `EXTRACTION_VERSION`, BECAUSE THEY GO STALE FOR DIFFERENT
REASONS AND ONLY ONE WAS TRACKED. `EXTRACTION_VERSION` says "the writer's
edge shape changed"; it says nothing about the VOCABULARY changing, and a
vocabulary change invalidates prior extractions just as thoroughly -- a term
that was quarantined as a `candidate_term` yesterday may be a canonical
material today.

That gap broke the loop the two-tier design promised. Promoting eight OPV
materials (PM6, Y6, DIO, ITO ...) and then asking `backfill_extractions` to
re-link the 23 papers that mention them SKIPPED 24 of them as
"already at version", because the writer version had not moved. Without this
stamp, `merge-novel` can enrich the vocabulary and the graph will never
notice.

Read from the loaded vocabulary rather than hardcoded, so a `merge-novel` run
is enough to invalidate the edges it affects -- no second constant to
remember to bump.

verified_symbols.name: link_section_entities
verified_symbols.doc:
Write one SECTION's entities. Replaces `link_paper_to_extractions`.

TWO BUGS ARE FIXED BY THE SIGNATURE ALONE.

First, it takes `SectionEntities` -- what THIS section yielded -- where the
old writer took the whole-paper `PaperExtraction` and was then called once
per section by all three of its callers. Every section therefore linked to
every technique the paper mentioned anywhere. That is what the live
5,813 describesTechnique edges over 285 nodes are: a cross-join, not
provenance. Section-level attachment is the only reason these edges hang off
sections at all, so attaching the paper aggregate to each one made the
structure assert something false.

Second, a non-canonical term gets a `candidate_term` node and a `mentions`
edge, never a `describes_*` one. `describes_technique` is a typed claim;
"this section named this string" is what extraction actually knows about a
term the vocabulary cannot place.

Materials are written for the first time (see `upsert_material`), also with
`mentions`: `forge:mentions` is glossed "this paper names that thing", and
extraction genuinely cannot tell "studied" from "referenced in passing". A
new `describes_material` predicate would claim a distinction the data does
not support -- and would land unmapped in `_PREDICATES`, the documented
failure mode.

Returns:
    Counts per kind, including ``candidates``. Unlike the old writer's
    ``materials``, every count here is real.
verified_symbols.signature: store: KGStore, pub_id: str, section_id: str, entities: SectionEntities, model_used: str | None=None, *, llm_ok: bool=False

verified_symbols.name: term_edges_for_sections
verified_symbols.doc:
Every term edge on the named sections, whatever its stamps say.

`term_edge_status` answers "what is out of date", which is the right question
almost always. This answers "what is there", which is what a FORCED redo
needs: those edges are current by every stamp, so the status sweep does not
list them, and leaving them in place would put the rewrite beside them with
the graph asserting both readings.

Separate function rather than a third return value from `term_edge_status`,
so that function's contract -- and its three callers -- stay untouched.

verified_symbols.name: term_edge_status
verified_symbols.doc:
Split this writer's edges into stale and current, keyed by SECTION.

THE RE-EXTRACTION BOOKKEEPING. Re-running extraction on a paper whose
sections already carry the OLD paper-level cross-join does not replace those
edges -- `upsert_edge` is idempotent now, so it ADDS the correct per-section
edges and LEAVES the wrong ones. The stale edges have to be deleted
explicitly, and this is what says which they are.

ONE SWEEP, NOT ONE QUERY PER SECTION. `mutations.find_links` is the
per-subject route and it is correct, but this corpus has 3,391 sections; a
query each is 3,391 round trips to answer a question one paged sweep of
33,145 edges already answers. The sweep also yields the properties, which is
where the version lives.

Accepts BOTH predicate spellings, because `TiledKGStore` stores
`forge:describesTechnique` while the SQLite store keeps the argument form
`describes_technique`. Matching one is the mistake that once read as "nothing
is linked" against 4,040 real edges.

Args:
    store: Open store; only `iter_edges` is used.
    version: The current writer version. Edges at or above it are done.

Returns:
    ``(stale_by_section, current_sections)``. The first maps a section's
    entity id to the opaque edge ids to delete; the second is the set of
    sections that already carry at-version edges, so a caller can skip their
    papers without re-reading anything.
verified_symbols.signature: store: KGStore, *, version: int=EXTRACTION_VERSION, vocabulary_version: int | None=None, require_llm: bool=False

verified_symbols.name: KGStore
verified_symbols.doc: Thread-safe SQLite knowledge graph store.

verified_symbols.name: get_store
verified_symbols.doc:
Return the module-level singleton graph store, creating it if needed.

Backed by the unified Tiled graph unless ``KG_BACKEND=sqlite`` is set.

The default flipped on 2026-08-13. The literature pipeline had been writing
publications, authors and materials into a private SQLite file while every
other entity in the system -- agent runs, simulations, fits, catalog
datasets -- lived in the Tiled entity/link graph, so "which papers relate
to this sample" spanned two stores sharing no identity and no query
surface. :class:`~als_knowledge_agent.graph.tiled_store.TiledKGStore`
presents this same interface over the Tiled graph, so no call site changed.

``KG_BACKEND=sqlite`` selects the old store. It exists for one purpose --
reading a graph built before the switch -- and is not a supported
configuration; the SQLite path retires once nothing needs to read the old
file (see docs/architecture/adr/ADR-002 for the equivalent decision on forge's side).

Args:
    db_path: SQLite file, used only by the legacy backend.

Returns:
    The singleton store.

verified_symbols.name: finite_properties
verified_symbols.doc:
Replace non-finite floats with None, recursively, before a graph write.

ONE NaN DESTROYS THE WHOLE EDGE, SILENTLY, AND BLAMES THE NETWORK. The write
path is `upsert_edge` -> `forge.kg.mutations.link_ids` -> `GraphQLClient.query`
-> `requests.post(json=...)`, and requests serialises with
``allow_nan=False``. A NaN therefore raises `InvalidJSONError`, which
subclasses `RequestException`, which the best-effort client catches and logs
as "GraphQL endpoint unreachable" before returning None. The link is dropped,
the simulation keeps no provenance at all, and the one message written
anywhere names the wrong cause.

NOT HYPOTHETICAL, IN TWO WRITERS. `paper_simulation` computes ratios
(`rod_metrics`, `_peak_vs_paper`) and `check_expected_peak` returns NaN for
every numeric field when the rendered q range does not reach the paper's
peak -- exactly the case a mapping fault produces, so the diagnostic most
worth recording is the one that would erase the record. `reduction_prov`
writes acquisition metadata and reduction settings straight off float
database columns, where an energy or an incident angle the beamline could
not read arrives as NaN.

It LIVES HERE, beside the writes it protects, rather than in
`paper_simulation`, which was its first home: that module costs 3.3 s to
import, which is not a price the reduction and live-session seams should pay
for a ten-line pure function. `paper_simulation._finite_properties` is now a
binding to this.

None is safe (it serialises to JSON null, and `rod_aspect_fwhm` already ships
it), and it carries the honest meaning: not measurable.

verified_symbols.name: relation_to_predicate
verified_symbols.doc:
CURIE for an als relation name.

Unknown relations become ``forge:<name>`` rather than raising: a pipeline
that invents an edge type should still write the edge.

THE FALLBACK IS A LAST RESORT, NOT A DESIGN. It emits the relation name
VERBATIM, so an unmapped `describes_technique` becomes
`forge:describes_technique` -- snake_case where every declared predicate is
camelCase, matching no constant, and silently absent from the viewer's
glossary (``views.ontology`` skips predicates with no ``PREDICATE_DOCS``
entry). Six relations were reaching the graph that way until 2026-08-18.
Anything written in quantity belongs in ``forge.kg.ontology`` with a gloss,
and mapped above.

verified_symbols.name: node_id_to_path
verified_symbols.doc:
The graph path for an als node id.

Args:
    node_id: An als node id, conventionally ``"<type>:<rest>"`` -- though a
        dataset's is a bare md5 hash with no prefix at all.
    entity_type: The node's type, which decides the keying rule.
    properties: The node's properties; the source of a dataset's real
        catalog path and of a publication's identifiers.

Returns:
    A path suitable for :func:`forge.kg.mutations.upsert_entity`.
verified_symbols.signature: node_id: str, entity_type: str='', properties: dict[str, Any] | None=None

verified_symbols.name: TiledKGStore
verified_symbols.doc:
``KGStore``'s interface, writing into the Tiled entity/link graph.

Not a subclass: it shares no implementation with the SQLite store, only its
method signatures. Instances are cheap; the expensive state is the entity-id
cache described below.

JSON remains a portable staging/snapshot format.

verified_symbols.name: graphql_endpoint_for
verified_symbols.doc:
Return the GraphQL POST endpoint for a graph server root.

Accepts a server root (``http://127.0.0.1:8011``), the API root
(``.../api``), or an endpoint that already names the route
(``.../api/graphql``), so a caller that has been configured with any of the

Args:

Returns:

verified_symbols.name: GraphQLClient
verified_symbols.doc:
Thin wrapper over a Tiled GraphQL endpoint.

Manages endpoint discovery, credential binding, query/mutation dispatch,
and best-effort semantics (unreachable endpoints return None, never raise).

Attributes:
    uri: Base URI of the GraphQL server (e.g., http://tiled:8011).
    api_key: Optional credential for authenticated endpoints.

verified_symbols.name: GraphQLClient.query
verified_symbols.doc:
Execute a GraphQL query.

Best-effort: returns None if the endpoint is unreachable. Logs a
warning but never raises.

Args:

    variables: Query variables, if any.

Returns:
    The response data dict, or None if the endpoint is unreachable or
    the response is malformed.

Raises:

        rejected by the server (errors present in response).

verified_symbols.name: GraphQLClient.mutation

Execute a GraphQL mutation.

Same semantics as query(): best-effort, returns None on unreachable

Args:

    variables: Mutation variables, if any.

Returns:
    The response data dict, or None if the endpoint is unreachable.
verified_symbols.signature: self, mutation_string: str, variables: dict[str, Any] | None=None

verified_symbols.name: GraphQLClient.mutations
verified_symbols.doc: Accessor for mutation operations.

verified_symbols.name: get_client
verified_symbols.doc:
Return a cached GraphQL client for a Tiled graph endpoint.

Session cache keyed by (uri, api_key), so multiple endpoints and
credentials coexist without cross-contamination.

Args:
    graph_uri: Tiled graph server URI (e.g., http://tiled:8011).
        Defaults to the configured tiled_graph_uri setting.
    api_key: Credential. Defaults to the configured graph_api_key.

Returns:
    A GraphQLClient instance.

Raises:

        host is not permitted by the Tiled host allowlist (raised by
        :class:`GraphQLClient`, which is where the check lives).

Example:
    Two calls with the same arguments return the same cached instance::

        client1 = get_client()
        client2 = get_client()
        assert client1 is client2
verified_symbols.signature: graph_uri: str | None=None, api_key: str | None=None

verified_symbols.name: clear_client_cache
verified_symbols.doc:
Drop every cached client.

Used in tests and for deployments that swap a server underneath a running

verified_symbols.name: warn_if_truncated
verified_symbols.doc:
Log when *rows* exactly fills *limit*, then return it unchanged.

Call it on the way out of a paged reader, wrapping the return value, so the
check cannot be forgotten separately from the return.

Args:
    rows: What the reader is about to return.
    limit: The bound it was given.
    reader: The reader's name, for the message -- the point is to name the
        function whose bound needs raising, not merely that something was
        capped.
    what: What is being counted, e.g. ``"paper_section entities"``.

Returns:
    ``rows``, unchanged. The return is passed through so this reads as
    ``return warn_if_truncated(rows, limit, "iter_links")`` rather than
    adding a statement a later edit can drop.
verified_symbols.signature: rows: list[T], limit: int, reader: str, what: str='rows'
